verified_ref: Kavita-Kaumudi vol. 1 (Ram Naresh Tripathi, 1918), 'Kabir Sahab' section, sakhi 71 (Hindi Wikisource transcription). Not found in the 'Binati kau ang' (petition) chapter of the Das Kabir Granthavali; no critical-edition locus found.
attribution_note: Reference checks out: the couplet is no. 71 in Tripathi's 1918 popular anthology, between two other petition couplets. But that anthology is a selection of Kabir-attributed sakhis with no manuscript apparatus, and I could not find the couplet in the Das Granthavali (the oldest-attested western collection). Britannica notes many couplets have been attributed to Kabir since his death. Confidence that it is Kabir's own: low to moderate; safe to present as 'attributed to Kabir'.
translation_note: Broadly right. 'तऊ पिता को लाज' means 'still, the honour (or shame) is the father's', i.e. the father's good name rides on the son. Our 'I am still my father's to look after' softens this; consider 'even so, the father's good name is bound up with me'. 'बकसु' = pardon (from Persian bakhsh); 'बाप जो' is likely the respectful 'Bapji/father'.
context: In Tripathi's anthology this couplet sits in a short run of petitions. Just before it the poet asks with what face he can plead when he does wrong in the Lord's very sight (70); just after, he says the Lord alone is merciful and all his running ends there, like a crow on a ship at sea that has no other perch (72). The ordering is the anthologist's, not necessarily Kabir's.

key_terms.sense: cherisher of the poor and humble; a title of God
a son, even an unworthy or wayward son
honour and good name, also shame: the father's reputation is at stake

core_teaching: The devotee owns his faults and asks pardon, appealing not to his merit but to the bond: a father's honour is tied to his child, even a bad one, so keeping the child is the father's own concern.

commentaries.gist: The neighbouring sakhis ask for the company of saints and the gift of compassion and humility, confess shame at sinning in God's sight, and call the Lord the only refuge, like a crow at sea with nowhere else to land.

commentaries.who: Ram Naresh Tripathi, introduction to the Kabir section (Kavita-Kaumudi, 1918)
commentaries.gist: Tripathi says Kabir wrote no books: he spoke sakhis and songs, disciples memorised them and they were compiled later; his couplets work almost like proverbs in everyday speech.

commentaries.who: Sung variant inside the bhajan 'नैया पड़ी मंझधार गुरु बिन कैसे लागे पार' (Kavitakosh)
commentaries.gist: The couplet survives in bhajan singing, reworded with Kabir's signature: the faults are servant Kabir's, the Lord cherishes the poor, and a father's name covers an unworthy son. There it frames the guru as ferryman.

Scholars work from three older collections (Dadu Panth Granthavali, Sikh Adi Granth, Kabir Panth Bijak); the oldest manuscripts are western, and Callewaert grades songs by their presence in early manuscripts and gives little weight to later bhajan collections.

practical_reading: For someone weighed down by guilt, the couplet shows a way to ask forgiveness from belonging rather than performance: you remain someone's child even when you have fallen short, and you can return on that basis.
misreadings: Not a licence to keep doing wrong because pardon is assured: the couplet before it is a confession of shame.
Not about a human father's duty to tolerate or cover up a child's wrongdoing.
'Father' is a relational image for God, not a sectarian doctrine; Kabir's God is also called Ram, Sain, Allah.
cautions: Father imagery can hurt readers whose father was absent, abusive or has recently died.
'Kaput' (bad son) is a harsh self-label; don't let the reading reinforce self-loathing in someone already full of shame.
Gendered (son/father) wording; the writer may need to widen it to 'child'.
speaks_to: feeling too unworthy to pray or ask for help
coming back after a long lapse
being the 'black sheep' of the family
not_for: readers estranged from or harmed by their father, unless reframed
situations needing accountability and repair toward someone the reader has hurt (the couplet is about being forgiven, not making amends)
research_note: No classical commentary exists. Printed locus: Tripathi 1918 only; also sung, reworded, as the sakhi of the bhajan 'नैया पड़ी मंझधार'. A popular-tradition sakhi; I could not confirm it in the Das Granthavali (only the Binati chapter was checked) or the Bijak.

verified_ref: Kabir Granthavali (Shyamsundar Das ed., western/Dadu Panth recension), 'Samrathai kau ang': sakhi 3 in the Kavitakosh transcription of that edition (which carries the edition's ख-manuscript notes and running total 606). It is numbered 1 only on a separate Kavitakosh selection page ('सम्रथाई का अंग / कबीर').
attribution_note: Belongs to the Granthavali, the western collection whose manuscripts are among the oldest for Kabir; Purushottam Agrawal calls it the most trustworthy source (per Lorenzen 2021). Confidence: moderate (individual sakhis can still not be proven). Fix the number: 'Samrathai kau ang 3' in the Das edition; '1' follows a popular selection page.
translation_note: Our text follows the selection page, which reads 'ना मरूम कोइ होइ' (no one is left mahrum, deprived) and has a typo 'तिस ब कोइ' (our 'तिस सब कोइ' is correct). The Das-edition transcription reads the last half as 'नाँव हरू मन होइ', which I could not construe and may be a transcription error; check against a print copy before quoting the second line as Kabir's. 'Empty-handed' is a fair rendering of mahrum.
context: The chapter is about God's all-sufficiency (samarthai). It opens with Kabir saying he did nothing and could do nothing; whatever was done, Hari did. This couplet follows: the one with nobody has God. Next comes the famous image that even with the seven seas as ink, every forest as pens and the earth as paper, God's qualities could not be written down; later, the Lord as a merchant who weighs the whole world without scales.

key_terms.term: जिसहि न कोई तिसहि तू (jisahi na koī tisahi tū)
key_terms.sense: whoever has no one has You

key_terms.term: जिस तू तिस सब कोइ (jis tū tis sab koi)

key_terms.sense: dargah: the court or threshold of a master

core_teaching: God is the refuge exactly of the friendless; whoever belongs to God finds everyone drawn to him; and no petitioner at the Lord's court is sent away with nothing.

commentaries.who: Kavitakosh bhavarth (volunteer gloss on the selection page)
commentaries.gist: Reads it as: when someone has no support anywhere, You alone are that support; once You are someone's, all others seek ties with him; nobody who reached Your court was ever turned away, all found shelter.

commentaries.who: Surrounding sakhis of 'Samrathai kau ang' (Das Granthavali text on Kavitakosh)
commentaries.gist: The chapter's theme is God's sole agency: Kabir did nothing, Hari did all; effort fails without Ram's help, every branch one steps on bends; the Lord turns a mustard seed into a mountain and back.
Places the Granthavali among the three older Kabir collections; its manuscripts are western and early, and Agrawal argues it is the most reliable source of Kabir's compositions.

practical_reading: For someone who feels utterly alone, the couplet says that having no one is the very condition in which God is nearest, and that no one is excluded from that court. Teachers often add its second claim: leaning on God tends to open human doors too.
misreadings: Not a guarantee that friends and family will reappear: 'whoever has You has everyone' is a spiritual claim, not a social promise.
Not a reason to refuse human help or community.
'Dargah' is a metaphor for God's court, not an endorsement of a particular shrine.
cautions: For a lonely reader who also feels God-forsaken, the line can sting; acknowledge the loneliness before offering the comfort.
Mixed Persian and Hindi devotional words (dargah, sain, mahrum): don't frame Kabir's God as narrowly Hindu or Muslim.
speaks_to: loneliness and having no one to turn to
migration or living far from family
after bereavement or a breakup leaves one without support
not_for: readers angry at God or in spiritual abandonment, where it may feel glib
someone in danger who first needs practical help
research_note: Second-half wording needs a print check of the Das Granthavali (Nagari Pracharini Sabha).

verified_ref: Closing line of the Rajasthani-form pada 'हेरी म्हा दरद दिवाणौ' (Kavitakosh page of that title). 'Kavitakosh 2' is not a Kavitakosh number. This is the same song as meera.kk.3 in a different dialect form; the Hindi form ends 'मीरां की प्रभु पीर मिटै जब वैद सांवलया होय' (Mira Vani, Rajkamal 2004, p. 26).
attribution_note: Traditional attribution only. No Mira manuscript survives from her lifetime; Hawley (as summarised by Melnikova 2018) found just six padas in pre-1700 manuscripts, and this is not one of them. The 'Mira' signature line does not by itself prove authorship. Firmly part of the sung Mira tradition; authorship by the historical Mira: unverifiable (confidence low).
translation_note: 'मीरा री प्रभु पीर मिटाँगा जब वैद साँवरो होय': 'Lord of Mira, the pain will ease when the Dark One is the physician.' 'Only' is implied by the pada (no physician has been found) but not stated; acceptable.
context: In its fuller form the song begins with Mira crazed with love and no one knowing her pain; only the wounded know a wound, only a jeweller knows a jewel; her bed is on a stake and her beloved's in the sky; she roams from forest to forest and finds no physician. This last line resolves it: the only healer is Krishna.
core_teaching: The ache of love in separation (viraha) is not something any ordinary remedy can treat; only the beloved Lord's presence heals it.

commentaries.who: Hindwi (Rekhta Foundation) prose gloss; text sourced to Mira Vani (Rajkamal Prakashan, 2004)
commentaries.gist: On the fuller Hindi form: she is lovesick and roams forest to forest finding no doctor; her pain will end only when the dark, lovely Krishna treats it himself.

commentaries.who: Rita Dubey and Rambaksh Jat, e-PG Pathshala (UGC/INFLIBNET) Hindi MA module 27, vyakhya of 'हेरी मैं तो दरध-दिवाणी'
commentaries.gist: The pain of not meeting the beloved is known only to Mira, and no physician can be found; it will go only when her Giridhar himself comes as the physician, because only he shares the experience.

commentaries.who: Nora Melnikova, 'Mirabai: a Saint or a Rebel?' (Cracow Indological Studies 20.2, 2018), summarising Hawley
commentaries.gist: The earliest-attested Mira padas speak only of love for Girdhar and the suffering of separation (viraha), with almost no biographical detail; this line belongs to that register.

practical_reading: Teachers use the image to say some heart-pain is not a problem to fix but a longing to be met. It can validate that an ache is real and turn the reader toward the source of love rather than numbing the pain.
misreadings: Not medical advice and not a reason to avoid doctors, therapy or medicine (our misuse note is right).
Not a claim that suffering proves holiness.
Not romantic advice to wait for a human partner to heal you.
cautions: Can be twisted into 'pray instead of getting treatment'; keep the misuse note visible.
Same song as meera.kk.3; do not use both in one plan without saying so.
speaks_to: a long ache nobody around understands
when advice and fixes have not helped
not_for: someone in acute medical or psychiatric crisis
a reader being pressured to 'just pray' instead of seeking care

verified_ref: Opening of the pada 'हे री मैं तो प्रेम-दिवानी मेरो दरद न जाणै कोय' (Kavitakosh 'मेरो दरद न जाणै कोय / मीराबाई'; also Mira Vani, Rajkamal 2004, p. 26, via Hindwi). Same song as meera.kk.2.
attribution_note: Traditional attribution only. No Mira manuscript survives from her lifetime; Hawley (as summarised by Melnikova 2018) found just six padas in pre-1700 manuscripts, and this is not one of them. The 'Mira' signature line does not by itself prove authorship. Firmly part of the sung Mira tradition; authorship by the historical Mira: unverifiable (confidence low). This is among the best-known Mira songs, but fame is not evidence of early attestation.
translation_note: Accurate for the Kavitakosh text. Versions differ in line order: in Mira Vani the 'wounded know the wounded' line comes after the 'bed on a stake / beloved's bed in the sky' lines and ends 'कि जिन लागी होय' (whoever has been struck). 'हे री' addresses a female companion. SETTING FLAG (minor): our setting and our_note say her family mocked her; the pada itself names no family. The academic gloss frames it as social constraints and a world that did not understand her, and family hostility comes from hagiography (Nabhadas; Shukla calls the poisoning a 'said' tradition). Suggest: 'Meera to a friend, on a pain of love no one around her understands.'
context: Mira speaks to a companion: she is mad with love and no one knows her pain. Only someone wounded knows a wound, only a jeweller a jewel. Her bed is on a stake, her beloved's in the sky, so how can they meet? She wanders forest to forest seeking a physician, and ends saying the pain will go only when Krishna is the physician.

key_terms.sense: jeweller: only an expert knows a jewel's worth
a bed on the impaling stake: unbearable torment

core_teaching: Love-longing is a wound only the wounded understand; Mira names her isolation and points to Krishna as the only cure.

commentaries.who: Hindwi (Rekhta Foundation) prose gloss; text sourced to Mira Vani (Rajkamal Prakashan, 2004)
commentaries.gist: Addressed to a sakhi: she is love-crazed and unknown in her pain; her bed is a stake while the beloved's is in the sky; only the wounded or a true jeweller understands; she roams finding no doctor until Krishna heals.

commentaries.who: Rita Dubey and Rambaksh Jat, e-PG Pathshala (UGC/INFLIBNET) Hindi MA module 27
commentaries.gist: Social bonds kept Mira from Krishna and the world missed her feeling. Real communication needs shared experience, so she forgives friend and foe alike: well-wishers advise from inexperience. Only Krishna knows this pain.

The earliest hagiography: Mira cast off public shame and the chains of family to worship Girdhar; the wicked tried to kill her with poison, which she drank like nectar. The family-hostility setting comes from this tradition, not from this pada.

Early sources give almost no biography beyond her leaving family ties and surviving poison; fuller details of her family life arrive only later, especially with Priyadas. Read biographical settings as tradition.

practical_reading: For someone whose pain feels invisible, the line affirms that only those who have been through it truly understand. That also explains, and lets one forgive, well-meant advice that misses the mark; it can nudge the reader toward people with lived experience, and devotionally toward bringing the pain to God.
misreadings: Not 'no one can ever help me': the song points to the one who can.
Not a romanticising of suffering.
Not evidence about Mira's family life.
cautions: Impaling-stake and wound imagery in the fuller pada is intense.
'Only the wounded know' can feed isolation in a depressed reader; pair it with an invitation to connect.
Duplicate song with meera.kk.2.
not_for: a reader in crisis who is withdrawing from everyone
anyone the line might convince that no one can understand them
research_note: Could not consult the Meera Brihat Padavali scan cited in verified_with.

verified_ref: Opening line of the pada titled 'राखौ कृपानिधान / मीराबाई' on Kavitakosh. 'Kavitakosh 4' is our internal number, not a Kavitakosh one.
attribution_note: Traditional attribution only. No Mira manuscript survives from her lifetime; Hawley (as summarised by Melnikova 2018) found just six padas in pre-1700 manuscripts, and this is not one of them. The 'Mira' signature line does not by itself prove authorship. Firmly part of the sung Mira tradition; authorship by the historical Mira: unverifiable (confidence low).
translation_note: Accurate. 'कृपा निधान' = treasury of grace/kindness; 'जी' is an honorific.
context: The pada goes on to list those the Lord has already saved: the sinner Ajamil, the elephant king drowning in the lake, the courtesan Ganika who rose to heaven, Kubja and the Bhil woman (Shabari); there are too many to count and the Vedas and Puranas tire of telling. It closes with Mira the servant taking refuge and asking the Lord to listen with both ears.
core_teaching: Mira surrenders and asks to be kept, resting her plea on the Lord's record of rescuing sinners and outcasts rather than on her own worth.

commentaries.gist: The plea is backed by precedent: Ajamil, Gajendra the elephant, Ganika, Kubja and Shabari were all saved though counted low or sinful; the list is endless, so Mira too may be kept.

commentaries.who: Nora Melnikova (Cracow Indological Studies, 2018), on the Mira corpus
commentaries.gist: Padas under Mira's name range widely in style and persona; the few early-attested ones are about love and separation, and this refuge-and-rescue song is not among them.

practical_reading: Teachers read it as permission to ask for help without credentials: everyone on the list was 'unworthy', so no one is too far gone to be held.
misreadings: Not passivity: taking refuge is an active choice.
The labels in the fuller pada ('नीच', 'अधम', 'गणिका') reflect period caste and gender attitudes, not an endorsement.
cautions: If quoting the fuller pada, the caste-laden word 'नीच' (low) is applied to Kubja and the Bhil woman; paraphrase with care.
not_for: a reader who needs to act against immediate danger; on its own it can read as passive waiting
research_note: Only one text witness found (Kavitakosh); no prose gloss located for this pada.

verified_ref: Verse 4, first half, of the pada 'प्रभु जी तुम दर्शन बिन मोय घड़ी चैन नहीं आवड़े' (Kavitakosh title 'प्रभु कब रे मिलोगे / मीराबाई'). 'Kavitakosh 5' is our internal number.
attribution_note: Traditional attribution only. No Mira manuscript survives from her lifetime; Hawley (as summarised by Melnikova 2018) found just six padas in pre-1700 manuscripts, and this is not one of them. The 'Mira' signature line does not by itself prove authorship. Firmly part of the sung Mira tradition; authorship by the historical Mira: unverifiable (confidence low). The phrase 'पंथ निहारूँ' is a stock formula in Mira songs (e.g. 'दरस बिन दूखन लागे नैन').
translation_note: Good. 'डगर भुवारूँ' = 'I sweep the path': the e-PG Pathshala text reads 'डगर बुहारूं' and glosses it as cleaning the road so his coming is easy. 'ऊभी' = standing (Rajasthani; that text has 'अभी', likely a variant or slip).
context: The pada: without your sight I get no peace for a moment; food and sleep desert me; I wander like a wounded woman and no one knows my pain; my days and nights are wasted, my life spent pining, my eyes worn out with weeping; had I known love brings such pain I would have beaten a drum through the town telling everyone not to love. Then this line: I watch the road and sweep the path. It ends asking when he will come, for meeting him is joy.

key_terms.sense: I sweep the path (readying for a guest)

core_teaching: Longing turned into readiness: she keeps the path swept and watches for the beloved, so the waiting becomes its own devotion.

commentaries.who: Rita Dubey and Rambaksh Jat, e-PG Pathshala (UGC/INFLIBNET) Hindi MA module 27, vyakhya of this pada
commentaries.gist: Mira addresses Krishna directly, mixing prayer, pain, reproach (upalambha), petition and longing. After saying she would have warned the town against love, she turns back to prayer: watching his road, sweeping it so his coming is easy.
The line comes after the song's lowest point (sleeplessness, wasted days, 'let no one love') and turns despair into active watching before the final hope that meeting him will be joy.

commentaries.who: Hindwi prose gloss on the parallel pada 'दरस बिन दूखन लागे नैन' (text sourced to Mira Vani, Rajkamal 2004)
commentaries.gist: The same 'watching the road' formula: with a fixed gaze she waits for him, the night of separation feels endless, and she has no one to tell her ache to.
Viraha, the lonely woman's longing for an absent beloved, is the core theme of the earliest Mira songs.

practical_reading: Teachers use the image for prayerful waiting that stays active: you cannot make the beloved come, but you can keep the path clean and keep looking. It suits anyone waiting on something they cannot hurry.
misreadings: Not a recommendation to put life on hold for someone.
Not a promise of when the waiting will end.
cautions: The same pada says she lost her life pining and wanted to warn everyone never to love; don't quote neighbouring lines to a heartbroken reader.
Not eating and not sleeping are named in the pada; the reading should not romanticise these.
speaks_to: waiting for someone to come home or call
not_for: fresh bereavement, where 'waiting for his return' can feed denial
someone waiting for an abusive partner to change

verified_ref: Lines 3-4 (with refrain) of the pada 'म्हारे घर आओ प्रीतम प्यारा' (Kavitakosh title 'तुम बिन नैण दुखारा / मीराबाई'); a variant is in Mira Vani (Rajkamal 2004, p. 131) as 'म्हाँरे घर आज्यो प्रीतम प्यारा'. Do not confuse with Kavitakosh's 'म्हारे घर / मीराबाई', a different pada ('म्हारे घर होता जाज्यो राज').
attribution_note: Traditional attribution only. No Mira manuscript survives from her lifetime; Hawley (as summarised by Melnikova 2018) found just six padas in pre-1700 manuscripts, and this is not one of them. The 'Mira' signature line does not by itself prove authorship. Firmly part of the sung Mira tradition; authorship by the historical Mira: unverifiable (confidence low).
translation_note: Accurate for the Kavitakosh text, but note: the forgiving clause 'तुम सा बगसणहारा' is only in that version. Mira Vani reads 'मैं त्रिगुणि गुण एक नाहीं तुझमें जी गुण सारा' (I have no merit; all merit is in you), with no forgiveness clause. Our 'line' therefore rests on one version. Our sanskrit field also splices two non-adjacent lines with the refrain between.
context: Mira begs the beloved to come to her house: she will offer body, mind and wealth and sing his praises. She sets his virtues against her faults, admits she has no merit, and ends asking when he will meet her, since her eyes ache without him.

key_terms.sense: the one who pardons and gives (Persian bakhsh)

core_teaching: Humility (dainya) before the Lord: she claims no merit and rests her hope on the beloved's generous nature.

commentaries.who: Hindwi (Rekhta Foundation) prose gloss; text sourced to Mira Vani (Rajkamal Prakashan, 2004)
commentaries.gist: Without the beloved the whole world tastes bitter; she will offer him everything; he is an ocean of virtues and she is full of faults with not one merit; she is miserable without his sight.
The refrain 'come to my house, beloved' frames each confession, so the admission of faults is an invitation, not a withdrawal; it closes on aching eyes and 'when will you meet me'.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for coming to God without a record of achievements: admit the gap honestly and invite the divine in anyway.
misreadings: Not self-hatred: the confession serves an invitation.
Not a statement that the reader is worthless.
cautions: 'All the faults are mine, all the virtue yours' can mirror the language of controlling relationships; frame it as humility before grace only.
Self-deprecation can reinforce low self-worth in a depressed reader.
not_for: readers with severe shame unless carefully framed
anyone in an abusive relationship where the self-blame pattern is already present

verified_ref: Opening of the pada 'तुम सुणो जी म्हारो अरजी' (Kavitakosh 'म्हारो अरजी / मीराबाई'); a near-identical version marked raga Darbari, tala Titala, with word glosses is at Kavitakosh 'तुम सुणौ दयाल म्हारी अरजी / मीराबाई'.
attribution_note: Traditional attribution only. No Mira manuscript survives from her lifetime; Hawley (as summarised by Melnikova 2018) found just six padas in pre-1700 manuscripts, and this is not one of them. The 'Mira' signature line does not by itself prove authorship. Firmly part of the sung Mira tradition; authorship by the historical Mira: unverifiable (confidence low).
translation_note: Accurate ('काढ़ो' = pull out; 'थारी मरजी' = as you will). SETTING FLAG: 'cut off by her own family' overstates. The pada says no one in the world is true kin except Raghubar (Rama) and that parents, family and clan are all self-interested; it does not describe being cut off. Suggest: 'Meera, finding no true kin in the world, asks the Lord to hear her.'
context: Mira pleads to be heard: she is being swept away in the ocean of worldly life, and asks to be pulled out if the Lord wills. No one in this world is truly hers; the true kinsman is Raghubar. Mother, father and clan all look after their own interest. She ends: hear Mira's plea and set her at your feet, as you will.
core_teaching: A cry for rescue that leaves the outcome to the Lord's will, made after human ties have proved unreliable.

commentaries.who: Kavitakosh word glosses (variant page, raga Darbari)
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'काढ़ो' as pull out, 'इण' as this, and 'गरजी' as selfish, supporting the reading that relatives act from self-interest while the Lord is asked to rescue.
Tradition remembers Mira breaking with family honour to worship Girdhar and surviving a poisoning attempt; this pada's complaint about kin is read against that story.

commentaries.who: Acharya Ramchandra Shukla, Hindi Sahitya ka Itihas (1929), via Hindwi
commentaries.gist: Shukla reports the legend that, harassed by relatives for keeping saints' company, Mira wrote to Tulsidas for advice, then rejects it as imagination since she died in samvat 1603. Family-conflict readings are tradition, not record.

practical_reading: For someone overwhelmed, it models a two-part prayer: say plainly that you are going under, then hand over the outcome. Teachers stress the second half: 'if you will' is trust, not resignation.
misreadings: Not a general verdict that families are selfish.
Not a reason to cut off family.
cautions: Calls parents and clan self-interested: may validate estrangement or wound a reader whose family is their support; quote only the plea in most plans.
Drowning imagery ('being swept away') for a reader with suicidal thoughts: pair with real-world help lines.
speaks_to: being overwhelmed or swept away by events
not_for: family-reconciliation plans
readers using 'drowning' language about their own life without added support

verified_ref: Opening lines of the pada 'तनक हरि चितवौ जी मोरी ओर' (Kavitakosh 'चितवौ जी मोरी ओर / मीराबाई').
attribution_note: Traditional attribution only. No Mira manuscript survives from her lifetime; Hawley (as summarised by Melnikova 2018) found just six padas in pre-1700 manuscripts, and this is not one of them. The 'Mira' signature line does not by itself prove authorship. Firmly part of the sung Mira tradition; authorship by the historical Mira: unverifiable (confidence low).
translation_note: Accurate. Note our 'line' adds editorial commentary ('Waiting without an answer is allowed to hurt'), which is not in the verse; keep it out of anything presented as a quotation.
context: Mira asks Hari to glance her way just a little: she keeps looking at him and he does not look back, so hard is his heart. Her hope rests on his glance alone; she has no other place. For her he is the only one, while he has millions like her. She has stood pleading so long that dawn has broken, and she ends by offering her life to the imperishable Lord.
core_teaching: Loving complaint to a Lord who seems not to answer: the devotee may say God seems hard and still keep all her hope there.

commentaries.gist: The complaint grows: for her he is everything, for him she is one of millions; she has pleaded all night till dawn; yet the song ends in self-offering, not anger.

commentaries.who: Rita Dubey and Rambaksh Jat, e-PG Pathshala (UGC/INFLIBNET) Hindi MA module 27 (on the related pada 'घड़ी अंक नहीं आवङै')
commentaries.gist: Describes Mira's direct address to Krishna as a blend of earnest prayer, statement of pain, reproach (upalambha), petition and longing; this pada is a pure case of that reproachful-loving mode.
Notes that Mira padas show her in many moods, from a desolate lover reaching out to an angry, scolding beloved; complaint against Krishna is a recognised strand of the corpus.

practical_reading: It gives permission to tell God that silence hurts. Teachers present it as honest prayer that keeps the relationship alive rather than quitting it.
misreadings: Not a claim that God is actually cruel.
Not a call to keep begging a person who ignores you.
cautions: The closing line 'देस्यूँ प्राण अकोर' (I will give my life as an offering) is devotional self-surrender, but could be misheard by someone with suicidal thoughts; do not quote it in distress plans.
Calling God hard-hearted can free some readers and unsettle others.
not_for: a reader with suicidal thoughts if the closing line is included
someone pining after a person who has clearly ended contact
research_note: Only one text witness found; no prose gloss of this exact pada located. The label 'upalambha' (our_note) is supported for Mira's address generally by the e-PG Pathshala module, though that module glosses a different pada.

verified_ref: Opening of the pada 'हरि मेरे जीवन प्राण अधार' (Kavitakosh 'प्राण अधार / मीराबाई'; also 'हरी मेरे जीवन प्रान अधार / मीराबाई', marked raga Hamir, with word glosses).
attribution_note: Traditional attribution only. No Mira manuscript survives from her lifetime; Hawley (as summarised by Melnikova 2018) found just six padas in pre-1700 manuscripts, and this is not one of them. The 'Mira' signature line does not by itself prove authorship. Firmly part of the sung Mira tradition; authorship by the historical Mira: unverifiable (confidence low).
translation_note: Accurate ('मंझार' = within; 'आसरो' = support). Note our 'line' drops Hari entirely ('there is still a support'), turning a devotional statement into a general one; fine as a gentle paraphrase but it is not what the verse says.
context: Hari is the support of her life and breath; in all three worlds she has no shelter but him. She has looked over the whole world and nothing pleases her without him. She ends: Mira is your servant, do not forget her.

key_terms.sense: the prop of life and breath

core_teaching: Hari is the one support that holds when nothing else does; the devotee asks only not to be forgotten.

commentaries.gist: Glosses 'आसरो' as support, 'मंझार' as in, 'रावरी' as yours: no support in the three worlds without you; I am your servant.
The refrain returns after each line, and the song closes with a plea not to be forgotten, so the statement of dependence ends as a request for remembrance.

commentaries.who: Rita Dubey and Rambaksh Jat, e-PG Pathshala (UGC/INFLIBNET) Hindi MA module 27 (parallel phrase in 'घड़ी अंक नहीं आवङै')
commentaries.gist: Glossing Mira's 'you are my life-breath', the module explains that Krishna is the support of her life and her very living rests on it; without him food and sleep leave her.

practical_reading: For someone whose usual supports have fallen away, it names a support that does not depend on circumstances; teachers pair it with the closing plea to be remembered.
misreadings: Not a rejection of human help or relationships.
Not a claim that nothing in the world has value.
cautions: 'No shelter but you' for a reader with no human supports: add encouragement to reach people too.
speaks_to: when every other support has failed
not_for: someone isolating themselves who needs to hear about human connection
research_note: No prose gloss of this exact pada beyond word meanings found.

verified_ref: Opening of the pada 'मन रे परसि हरि के चरन' (Kavitakosh page titled, with a typo, 'मन रे पासि हरि के चरन / मीराबाई'; the text reads 'परसि').
attribution_note: Traditional attribution only. No Mira manuscript survives from her lifetime; Hawley (as summarised by Melnikova 2018) found just six padas in pre-1700 manuscripts, and this is not one of them. The 'Mira' signature line does not by itself prove authorship. Firmly part of the sung Mira tradition; authorship by the historical Mira: unverifiable (confidence low).
translation_note: Accurate. 'परसि' = touch; 'त्रिविध ज्वाला' = the threefold fire. Our 'line' turns 'touch' into 'rest at', which is a soft but acceptable paraphrase.
context: Mira tells her own mind to touch Hari's feet, lovely, cool and lotus-soft, which take away the threefold fire. The pada then lists what those feet did: Prahlad touched them and gained Indra's rank (Shukla's text), Dhruva was made immovable by them, they spanned the universe, freed Gautama's wife (Ahalya), and lifted Govardhan to humble Indra's pride. It ends calling Girdhar the one who carries others across.

key_terms.sense: removing the threefold fire (the three kinds of suffering)

core_teaching: Turning the restless mind toward the Lord's feet cools every kind of burning suffering, as it did for Prahlad, Dhruva and Ahalya.

commentaries.gist: The comfort is grounded in stories: the same feet raised Prahlad, steadied Dhruva, freed Ahalya and humbled Indra, so the mind is urged to seek them.

commentaries.who: Acharya Ramchandra Shukla, Hindi Sahitya ka Itihas (1929), Krishna-bhakti section, via Hindwi
commentaries.gist: Shukla prints this as one of two representative Mira padas. He describes her worship as madhurya bhava, Krishna as beloved or husband, and notes her padas are partly Rajasthani-mixed, partly literary Braj, all absorbed in love.

commentaries.who: Tulsidas, Ram Rajya passage (Ramcharitmanas), with gloss from Pushp-Parag (ed. Tekchand Shastri), via Hindwi
commentaries.gist: Names the three kinds of suffering (daihik, daivik, bhautik) and glosses them as bodily illness like fever, calamity like famine, and harm from creatures; this is the 'threefold fire' Mira says the feet remove.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as a self-talk practice: when the mind is burning with anxiety, anger or worry, deliberately direct it to a cooling, steady image of the divine.
misreadings: Not a promise that physical or circumstantial suffering will vanish.
Not a substitute for treatment of anxiety disorders.
cautions: Prahlad and Dhruva stories involve child abuse and rejection by a parent; if the reading expands on them, keep that in mind.
not_for: readers who need practical steps rather than contemplation in an emergency
research_note: Shukla's text is better than Kavitakosh's in places ('इंद्र पदवी धरन', 'ब्रह्मांड भेट्यो', 'अगम तारन तरन'); prefer it if quoting more of the pada. No line-by-line gloss of this pada found.

verified_ref: The pada 'पायो जी म्हें तो राम रतन धन पायो' (Kavitakosh page of that title). Mira Vani (Rajkamal 2004, p. 112, via Hindwi) reads the opening as 'मैंने नाम रतन धन पायौ' (the jewel-wealth of the Name).
attribution_note: Traditional attribution only. No Mira manuscript survives from her lifetime; Hawley (as summarised by Melnikova 2018) found just six padas in pre-1700 manuscripts, and this is not one of them. The 'Mira' signature line does not by itself prove authorship. Firmly part of the sung Mira tradition; authorship by the historical Mira: unverifiable (confidence low). The unnamed satguru is identified with Raidas (Ravidas) only by later tradition; the Raidas link goes back to Anantadas's Raidas parchai (c. 1665), where a Jhali queen of Chittaur, later identified with Mira, takes initiation from him (Melnikova 2018). Do not name Raidas as fact.
translation_note: Accurate. 'राम रतन' vs 'नाम रतन' varies by edition; our 'jewel-wealth of Ram's name' covers both. 'सवायो' = growing by a quarter, i.e. increasing.
context: Mira rejoices: she has found the jewel of Ram's name, a priceless thing given by her true guru, who in kindness made her his own. It is the capital of many lives; she lost all that the world counts. It does not run out when spent, thieves cannot take it, it grows each day. With truth as the boat and the guru as boatman she has crossed the ocean of becoming, and sings his praise with joy.

key_terms.sense: the jewel-wealth of Ram (or 'of the Name')

core_teaching: The Name received through the guru's grace is a wealth that grows by being spent and that nothing can take away; worldly losses are small beside it.

commentaries.who: Hindwi (Rekhta Foundation) prose gloss; text sourced to Mira Vani (Rajkamal Prakashan, 2004)
commentaries.gist: She has found Ram's wealth; the satguru kindly adopted her and gave a priceless thing; losing the world she gained the wealth of births; it cannot be spent or stolen; the guru rows truth's boat across.

commentaries.who: Nora Melnikova (Cracow Indological Studies, 2018), on the guru tradition
commentaries.gist: The Raidas-as-guru link grows from Anantadas's story of a Chittaur queen initiated by Raidas, later identified with Mira; modern devotional writers make it central. Treat the guru's identity as tradition.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to contrast inner wealth with outer: what is found in practice and grace cannot be stolen or used up. It suits readers after financial or material loss.
misreadings: Not a money or prosperity promise (our misuse note is right).
Not contempt for honest work or wealth; 'lost all the world's' is about attachment.
cautions: 'Lost everything in the world' can feel flip to someone in real financial hardship; acknowledge the loss first.
speaks_to: after financial loss or job loss
not_for: readers in acute poverty if framed as 'money doesn't matter'

verified_ref: Line 3 of the pada 'कोई कहियौ रे प्रभु आवन की' (Kavitakosh 'कोई कहियौ रे / मीराबाई'; also Mira Vani, Rajkamal 2004, p. 40, via Hindwi).
attribution_note: Traditional attribution only. No Mira manuscript survives from her lifetime; Hawley (as summarised by Melnikova 2018) found just six padas in pre-1700 manuscripts, and this is not one of them. The 'Mira' signature line does not by itself prove authorship. Firmly part of the sung Mira tradition; authorship by the historical Mira: unverifiable (confidence low).
translation_note: Accurate. Listener: the pada addresses 'कोई' (anyone, someone), not a specific friend; 'a friend' is close enough but 'anyone who will listen' is more exact.
context: Mira asks someone, anyone, to bring word that the Lord is coming. He neither comes nor writes; he has a habit of keeping her hoping. Her eyes won't obey her and stream like monsoon rivers. She is helpless and has no wings to fly to him. She ends: when will you meet me? I have become your servant, caught in your snare.

key_terms.sense: will not obey what I say
the monsoon month; byword for heavy rain

key_terms.term: बाण पड़ी ललचावन की (bāṇ paṛī lalchāvan kī)
key_terms.sense: he has got into the habit of keeping me hoping

core_teaching: Tears in waiting are not a failure of will; the longing for the beloved overflows on its own.

commentaries.who: Hindwi (Rekhta Foundation) prose gloss; text sourced to Mira Vani (Rajkamal Prakashan, 2004)
commentaries.gist: Someone tell me the Lord is coming; he neither comes nor sends a letter, and keeps tempting me; my eyes won't listen; I am helpless and have no wings; when will you meet me, I am caught in your toils.
The monsoon image sits between 'he does not even write' and 'I have no wings to fly to him': the tears are the body's answer to helplessness, not drama.

commentaries.who: Rita Dubey and Rambaksh Jat, e-PG Pathshala (UGC/INFLIBNET) Hindi MA module 27 (general observation on Mira's padas)
commentaries.gist: Mira never describes the experience of meeting God; her songs voice the wish and the faith that meeting will surely come, but in the padas it never actually happens.

practical_reading: It gives permission to cry. For someone who cannot stop tearing up, the line says the eyes have their own will and that is human, not weakness.
misreadings: Not a call to keep waiting for someone who has stopped writing back.
cautions: 'He neither comes nor writes' can sharply touch readers ghosted by a partner or estranged from a child; may comfort or reopen a wound.
not_for: readers who need to move on from a relationship, if framed as 'keep waiting'

verified_ref: Rahim-Kavitavali (1926), Dohe no. 61 (Hindi Wikisource). Kavitakosh 'Rahim Dohavali - 2' gives it as no. 72 with a variant.
attribution_note: Text and number match Rahim-Kavitavali (ed. Surendranath Tiwari, 1926) on Hindi Wikisource. The editor himself says no old manuscript of Rahim's dohas was available, copying has corrupted wording, and some dohas' sense is unclear. Kavitakosh's 'Rahim Dohavali' numbers differ. Confidence: traditional attribution, moderate.
translation_note: Reading differs by edition: 1926 has 'तन-मन दियो' (gave body and mind), Kavitakosh has 'तन मन लियो' (took body and mind). Either way the beloved is the one who has one's whole self and lives in the heart, so our sense holds. Grammatically 1926 is most naturally 'the one to whom Rahim gave body and mind'; our 'to the one who has been given body and mind' fits that. NB: the '1926 edition footnotes' cited in verified_with do not exist for this doha.
context: In the 1926 edition the dohas are arranged alphabetically, so there is no thematic context. The editor counts about 17 devotional and 11 love (shringar) dohas among some 250; our note reads this one as devotional, though it fits human love equally.

key_terms.sense: gave (or took) body and mind: total self-giving
a home made inside the heart

key_terms.term: रही बात अब कौन (rahī bāt ab kaun)
key_terms.sense: what is left to say now?

core_teaching: When the beloved already lives in the heart, nothing needs reporting: one's joys and sorrows are already known.

commentaries.gist: Tiwari describes Rahim as generous, patient and deeply trusting in God, and sorts his dohas: mostly ethical maxims, with a smaller group of devotional and love dohas. This one sits at that devotion-love border.
The variant 'took body and mind' makes the beloved the active one who has claimed the poet and settled in his heart, which sharpens the point that nothing remains to be told.

practical_reading: For someone who cannot find words to pray, it says you do not need them: the one who lives in your heart already knows. It also fits a close human bond where explanations are unnecessary.
misreadings: Not advice to stop talking to a partner because 'they should just know'.
Not a reason to hide one's troubles from people who can help.
cautions: For a reader whose loved one has died, 'the one in your heart already knows' can comfort or ache; use gently.
not_for: relationship conflict where communication is the actual need
research_note: No commentary on this specific doha found.

verified_ref: Rahim-Kavitavali (1926), Dohe no. 89 (Hindi Wikisource). Kavitakosh 'Rahim Dohavali - 2' no. 103.
attribution_note: Text and number match Rahim-Kavitavali (ed. Surendranath Tiwari, 1926) on Hindi Wikisource. The editor himself says no old manuscript of Rahim's dohas was available, copying has corrupted wording, and some dohas' sense is unclear. Kavitakosh's 'Rahim Dohavali' numbers differ. Confidence: traditional attribution, moderate. CAUTION: a near-identical doha is attributed to Hariram Vyas (16th-c. Vrindavan poet) with the signature 'व्यास': 'व्यास दीनता पारसै ... दीन भये तैं मिलत है, दीनबंधु से बंध' (Hindwi, citing Bholanath Tiwari, Hindi Niti-Kavya-Dhara, 1984). Shared or floating authorship is possible; present as 'attributed to Rahim'.
translation_note: Acceptable. 'भली बिचारी दीनता' can be read 'poor humility is good' or 'humility, on reflection, is good'; either way humility is praised because it brings a kinsman like Dinabandhu. 'Divine sweetness' renders 'दिव्य ... रस' well. SETTING FLAG: 'humility after a fall' imports Rahim's biography (his property was seized and he became poor under Jahangir, per the 1926 introduction); the doha itself does not mention a fall. Fine as framing if labelled tradition.
context: Alphabetical placement in the 1926 edition; the very next doha (90) continues the thought: the lowly man watches everyone but no one watches him, and whoever does look after the lowly becomes like Dinabandhu, the Friend of the lowly.
core_teaching: Lowliness has a hidden sweetness the world cannot see: it makes God, the Friend of the lowly, one's own kin.

commentaries.gist: The paired doha shifts from receiving to giving: the poor notice everyone but are noticed by none; whoever does notice them becomes like Dinabandhu himself.

Tiwari recounts that after Akbar's death Rahim's property was seized and he wandered in poverty, still besieged by petitioners, and reads several dohas as voicing that experience and his trust in God.

commentaries.who: Hariram Vyas parallel (Hindwi, from Bholanath Tiwari, Hindi Niti-Kavya-Dhara, 1984)
commentaries.gist: Vyas's version: the blind world does not know that humility is a philosopher's stone; by becoming lowly one gains a kinsman like Dinabandhu. Same idea, different signature.

practical_reading: For someone brought low by failure, illness or loss of status, it suggests that the lowered place is where God draws near and where one learns to see others who are low.
misreadings: Not a call to accept humiliation or abuse (our misuse note is right).
Not praise of poverty as such.
cautions: Telling someone freshly humiliated that lowliness is 'sweet' can sound dismissive; lead with their pain.
speaks_to: after a public failure or demotion
not_for: readers being bullied or abused, where 'humility' could be misheard as 'accept it'

verified_ref: Rahim-Kavitavali (1926), Dohe no. 91 (Hindi Wikisource). Kavitakosh 'Rahim Dohavali - 2' no. 106 ('धरत रहीम न धीर').
attribution_note: Text and number match Rahim-Kavitavali (ed. Surendranath Tiwari, 1926) on Hindi Wikisource. The editor himself says no old manuscript of Rahim's dohas was available, copying has corrupted wording, and some dohas' sense is unclear. Kavitakosh's 'Rahim Dohavali' numbers differ. Confidence: traditional attribution, moderate.
translation_note: Plausible but the first line is ambiguous: 'धरैं रहीम न धीर' can mean people do not keep their composure (they laugh) or do not offer steadiness. Our 'do not keep you steady' picks one reading. The second line ('कही सुनैं सुनि-सुनि करैं, ऐसे वे रघुवीर') clearly praises Raghuvir as one who hears and then acts. No published gloss found to settle line one.
context: Alphabetical placement in the 1926 edition. The thought echoes Rahim's better-known counsel elsewhere to keep one's sorrow to oneself because people will only mock it; here the alternative is given: tell it to Raghuvir, who listens and helps.

key_terms.sense: the hero of the Raghu line: Rama

core_teaching: People may mock your sorrow; Rama hears it and, having heard, helps.

commentaries.gist: Tiwari stresses Rahim's full trust in God, quoting dohas where he leaves every matter to the Lord and does not fear in war, forest, sickness or calamity because the one who kept him in the womb still keeps him.

Rahim's companion counsel: keep the ache of your heart hidden, because people who hear it will only make fun and none will share the load. Doha 91 supplies the other half: there is one listener who does not mock.
Gives the same doha with 'धरत' for 'धरैं', confirming the wording apart from that verb form.

practical_reading: For someone who has been laughed at or dismissed after sharing pain, it says there is one listener who does not mock and who acts. Writers can add: also find the people who listen like that.
misreadings: Not advice never to share sorrow with people.
Not a claim that everyone mocks suffering.
cautions: Could reinforce 'no one cares' for a reader already isolated; pair with encouragement to find safe listeners.
speaks_to: being mocked or dismissed after opening up
not_for: readers who need to be urged toward therapy or friends, if framed as 'tell only God'
research_note: No gloss found for this doha; the first line's sense is uncertain.

verified_ref: Rahim-Kavitavali (1926), Dohe no. 193 (Hindi Wikisource). Kavitakosh 'Rahim Dohavali - 5' no. 252 ('यहै जान अवतार').
attribution_note: Text and number match Rahim-Kavitavali (ed. Surendranath Tiwari, 1926) on Hindi Wikisource. The editor himself says no old manuscript of Rahim's dohas was available, copying has corrupted wording, and some dohas' sense is unclear. Kavitakosh's 'Rahim Dohavali' numbers differ. Confidence: traditional attribution, moderate.
translation_note: Acceptable as ONE reading, but stated too firmly. Line one is clear. Line two is unglossed in every source I found and can be read: (a) knowing this, God takes avatar (our reading, taking जानि as 'having known'); (b) know this remembrance to be itself an avatar, a real coming-near; (c) know that this is what birth is for. Mark ours as interpretive. LINE FLAG: our 'line' ('People who were parted do meet again') turns the doha into a flat promise, which can read as a promise of reunion with the dead; soften to 'remembering again and again brings the parted near'.
context: Alphabetical placement in the 1926 edition. The editor notes that some of Rahim's dohas have unclear sense because of copying errors; this one's second line is a likely example.
core_teaching: Repeated remembrance is the best thing there is: through it, those who have been parted come together again.

commentaries.gist: Tiwari warns that no old manuscript of the dohas was found, that copying has loosened language and sense, and that several dohas' meaning is not clear; read line two of this doha with that caution.
Same doha with 'यहै जान अवतार' and 'मिलें', confirming the wording; it offers no gloss.

practical_reading: For someone missing a person, it honours remembering as a real form of closeness, something that can bring the absent near.
misreadings: Not a promise that the dead will physically return or that a lost relationship will be restored.
Not a doctrine about why avatars happen.
cautions: 'The separated meet again' can be read as reincarnation or afterlife reunion; with fresh grief this may comfort or feel like a promise the text does not make.
speaks_to: hope of reunion after a rift
not_for: fresh bereavement if framed as a promise of reunion
readers trying to let go of a harmful relationship
research_note: No gloss found; second line's meaning unsettled.
